hints: Notice the first voltmeter reading of $9.000\text{ V}$ is with no $11.0\text{ }\Omega$ resistor connected, so no load current flows and it equals the e.m.f. $E$ of the battery.

Connect the second reading of $8.800\text{ V}$ to the $11.0\text{ }\Omega$ resistor now in parallel with the battery, so use $I = V/R$ with $V = 8.800\text{ V}$ to get the current leaving the battery.
Use the lost volts $E - V = 0.200\text{ V}$ and the relation $E - V = Ir$ to solve for the internal resistance $r$ inside the dashed box.
walkthrough: The voltmeter draws negligible current, so the first reading with no external $11.0\text{ }\Omega$ resistor is the e.m.f.: $E = 9.000\text{ V}$.
When the $11.0\text{ }\Omega$ resistor is connected, the voltmeter reads the terminal p.d.: $V = 8.800\text{ V}$. The same $V$ is across the $11.0\text{ }\Omega$ load.
Find the load current using $I = V/R$: $I = 8.800/11.0 = 0.800\text{ A}$. This current must have come through the internal resistance.
State the terminal p.d. equation $V = E - Ir$, so the voltage lost inside the battery is $E - V = Ir$.
Substitute values with units: $9.000\text{ V} - 8.800\text{ V} = 0.200\text{ V} = 0.800\text{ A} \times r$.
Rearrange: $r = 0.200/0.800 = 0.250\text{ }\Omega$, with correct resistance units and small value expected for a battery. This is option B.

options.A: This uses $9.000\text{ V}$ instead of $8.800\text{ V}$ to find the current in the $11.0\text{ }\Omega$ resistor, giving $I = 9.000/11.0$ and a slightly small $r$.
options.B: The lost volts $9.000-8.800 = 0.200\text{ V}$ divided by the load current $8.800/11.0 = 0.800\text{ A}$ gives $r = 0.250\text{ }\Omega$.
options.C: This is near $11.0 \times 8.8/9.0$ and treats the $11.0\text{ }\Omega$ load and internal resistance incorrectly as a potential divider for $8.8\text{ V}$.
options.D: This is near $11.0 \times 9.0/8.8$ and inverts the terminal p.d. and e.m.f. relationship for the internal resistance.
